# Tree-based thinking

In our simulation exercises, we have so far focused on learning the ins and outs
of _slendr_ --- how to construct demographic models, how to compute summary
statistics, and how exploratory, simulation-based workflows can help us to study
their behavior and limitations. Hopefully, you got a useful glimpse of how
empowering simulation-based exploration is and how easily the approaches shown
can be extended to other software methods and other kinds of models (something
you will get to practice much more towards the end of our workshop).

In this chapter, we will play with _slendr_ an interactive "popgen calculator"
to quickly explore ideas and build intuition into how (and why) some more
complex statistics work, specifically in the context of tree-sequences (or,
sometimes, ancestral recombination graphs).

Unlike the previous chapters, which involved a lot of guidance and explanation
to make sure you understand how _slendr_ operates (and why), this chapter will
be a bit more compressed and focused on interesting and useful bits of
functionality to push your modeling with _slendr_ even further.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

library(dplyr)   # manipulating tabular data
library(ggplot2) # data visualization
library(cowplot) # composing plots into panels
library(purrr)   # convenient looping functions
```










## Exercise: $f_4$ as a measure of "overlapping paths" through a tree

We will begin by exploring perhaps the most critical component of population
genetics research (particularly in the context of ancient DNA genomics)---the
venerable $f-4$-statistic, [formally established by Nick Patterson and David
Reich](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/192/3/1065/5935193).

**Create a new script `f_statistics.R` and paste the following code into that
script. Then, as always, read through the code, try to decipher what it's going
to do, then run it and compare your understanding with the visualization of the
model.**

```{r}
#| output: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

p4 <- population("p4", time = 4000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)
schedule <- schedule_recording(
  model, times = 0,
  list(p1, 5), list(p2, 5), list(p3, 2), list(p4, 1)
)

plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

# writing `samples` over and over gets annoying, so let's switch that to `s`
s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

::: aside

**Note:** I numbered the population the "reversed way" because it makes more
sense to my brain with regards to how $f_4$ quartets are often arranged.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### click to see the solution

```{r}
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)
```

:::


**Given the phylogenetic relationships between the populations encoded by our
model, what value would you expect for $f_4(p1, p2; p3, p4)$? try to guess first
without any coding, then compute the statistic with the `ts_f4()` function. does
your simulation give you the result you might expect based on logic alone? if
not, why could this be?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### click to see the solution

As we can see below, $f$-statistics theory tells us that the value should be
zero, but without any reference point, we get a number which is very tiny (the
value in the `f4` column), but how tiny would it have to be to be "basically
zero"?

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
```

The reason we didn't get _exactly_ zero is stochasticity, and the fact that
along a genome (even a small one, only 10 Mb of simulated sequence) there are
many possible trees. Sometimes, [incomplete lineage
sorting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incomplete_lineage_sorting) will lead to
genealogical trees which do not fit the tidy, well-behaved population tree like
the one we see when we run `plot_model()`.

:::

---

As suggested in the solution above, the reason we don't get a perfectly zero
expected value of the $f_4$ is because of ILS and stochasticity. Let's test this
hypothesis now.

**First, evaluate `ts` in your R console and note how many individual trees do you
have in your 10 Mb tree-sequence.**

**Now, restart your R session (`Session -> Restart R`). Then, temporarily change
the $N_e$ of all lineages in your model to 1 and re-run your script to get a new
`ts` and compute the same $f_4$ statistic again. $N_e$ of one implies
ridiculously high amount of drift, which should eliminate ILS completely, giving
us $f_4$ close to its mathematical expectation of zero. Is this true? How many
trees does your tree sequence have now?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| echo: false
ts_num_trees <- ts$num_trees
```

We changed all N sizes to 1, then we rerun the entire script `f_statistics.R`
again:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

#
# note the change to N = 1 !!!
#
p4 <- population("p4", time = 4000, N = 1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 3000, N = 1, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)
schedule <- schedule_recording(
  model, times = 0,
  list(p1, 5), list(p2, 5), list(p3, 2), list(p4, 1)
)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

Now let's compute the $f_4$ again on the `ts` tree sequence produced by this
extreme model:

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
```

Indeed, when we type `ts` into the R console, we see that it only contains `{r}
ts$num_trees` individual trees compared to the previous count of `{r}
ts_num_trees`, consistent with an absolutely extreme amounts of genetic drift in
your model.

:::

---

Of course, changing $N_e$ to value of 1 as we did above is a drastic measure of
generally only theoretical utility. We could hardly get away with doing that, if
we wanted to use simulations to make a point in our research paper.

How do we deal with the unavoidable stochasticity in our simulations then? This
wasn't much of a problem in exercises in the previous chapters, but we need the
way to solve this to be able to get useful, applicable results.

Let's look into this now.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| echo: false
p4 <- population("p4", time = 4000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

:::






## Exercise: Reducing stochastic noise via simulation replicates

As a means to tame the stochasticity and help meaningful statistical patterns
stand out, I recently implemented a function `ts_replicates()`. The way it works
is like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts_replicate(
  n = <number of replicates>,
  {
    # ...
    # a block of slendr code wrapped in { ... } containing a ts simulation
    # and a slendr statistical computation we want to run in replicates
    # ...
  }
)
```

---

**Take a look at its manual page under `?ts_replicates`, then use it to run 10
replicate simulations of the $f_4$ statistic above** (the one which should give
us a zero expectation, but it wasn't clear if it did or not), **saving it to
variable `df`. What format does the result have? When you visualize the
distribution of $f_4$ values across all replicates, are they more understandable
in terms of the statistical expectation for this particular $f_4$ quartet?**

::: aside

**Note:** If you want to speed up the replicate simulation, not that
`?ts_replicate` describes the means to run multiple simulations in parallel.

:::

::: aside

**Note:** I wrote this function a few days ago in a bit of a haste, specifically
for this workshop, but also hoping it'll be useful in daily research. Feedback
appreciated!

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's how we can tweak the "template" above to answer the question:

```{r}
df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 20, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
})
```

We can see that we get the same format of the data frame as normally produced by
the `ts_f4()` function, except with a new column `rep` added, indicating a
replicate number.

```{r}
df
```

This means we can visualize their distribution easily like this, for example:

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")
```

As we can see, when we run multiple replicates of the simulation, we are able
to "control" the stochastic noise a bit, making the expected pattern stand out
more clearly: we see that the expected value of `{r} unique(df$statistic)`
is really zero.

:::

---

**Why do we put the `ts <- ...` simulation code inside the `ts_replicate()` block?
What happens when you only run the `ts_f4()` command in the `{ ... block ... }`
inside `ts_replicate()`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's run the `ts_replicate()` without (internally) simulating the tree sequence:

```{r}
df_bad <- ts_replicate(n = 20, {
  ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
})
```

When we do this, we can see that we got the same value throughout! This is because
all replicates are computed on the same outcome of a single evolutionary process
which generated the tree-sequence object `ts`.

This is unlike the correct way of using `ts_replicate()`, which simulates an
independent `ts` object for each replicate, each of those then being based on an
independent realization of the demographic model in question.

:::








## Exercise: Mutations versus branches

Do you recall how I told you earlier that you don't have to add mutations to
your tree sequence `ts`, and still be able to compute population genetic
statistics? But that you can safely add them with `ts_mutate()` anyway?

The reason this works is because some very smart people figured out a
mathematical [duality between mutation-based and branch-based
statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/215/3/779/5930459)---it
actually doesn't matter which way we compute our statistics, they give
mathematically the same result.

On a practical level, we usually resort to mutation-based computation, which is
how _slendr_ statistical functions operate by default. But population genetics
theory (described in the paper in detail) suggests that branch-based computation
is less noisy than mutation-based computation.

Let's test to what degree is this the case.

---

**Modify your `ts_replicate()` command so that it internally produces two data
frames:**

1. **`df_mutations` --- computed with `ts_f4()` same as before, except that you
should add a new column to this data frame called `mode` with the value `"mutataions"`,**

2. **`df_branches` --- computed with `ts_f4()` by additionally setting its
argument `mode = "branch"`, and adding a new column to this data frame called `mode` with the value `"branches"`.**

**The last thing your `ts_replicate()` command should do is to combine them into
a single data frame with `rbind(df_mutations, df_branches)`.**

**Now visualize the distributions of $f_4$` values between the two variations of
`ts_f4()` computation you just did. Is one of them noisier than the other? If
so, why could this be?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the complete modified script `f_statistics.R` with the expanded solution
to this exercise:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p4 <- population("p4", time = 4000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 5), list(p2, 5), list(p3, 2), list(p4, 1))

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 20, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(model, split = TRUE, schedule = schedule)

  df_mutations <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
  df_mutations$mode <- "mutations"

  df_branches <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch")
  df_branches$mode <- "branches"

  rbind(df_mutations, df_branches)
})
```

Let's visualize the results for comparison between mutation-based and
branch-based computation:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(mode, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ mode, scales = "free_y")
```

Do you see a massive difference in the variance between both batches of
simulations? I personally don't. This suggests that, particularly because it
makes comparisons of our simulations to real-world software methods (which all
work on mutations) easier, in a general case we might as well stick to
mutation-based computation.

See [this
tutorial](https://tskit.dev/tutorials/no_mutations.html#genealogy-based-measures-are-less-noisy)
(and particularly the directly linked section) for more explanation on this
topic.

:::










## Exercise: "Outgroup" $f_3$ as a measure of overlap of tree paths

To ease into the problem of interpreting $f$-statistics as measures of
overlapping paths in "population trees" (or, when admixture comes into the
picture), in "population graphs", let's get back to our familiar $f_3$
statistic.

Consider the model from our script `f_statistics.R`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule)
```

We know from [the theory of
$f$-statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/202/4/1485/5930214)
that the $f_2$ statistic measures the branch length between two samples (two
individuals, or groups of individuals)---see equation (1) in the linked paper.

Another thing established in the paper is the fact that any $f$-statistic can be expressed as a
linear combination of $f_2$ statistics.

For instance, equation 20b in the same paper states the following:

$$f_3(A; B, C) = \frac{1}{2} (f_2(A, C) + f_2(A, B) - f_2(B, C))$$

**Draw a doodle of the population model above on a piece of paper which traces
the paths indicated by the $f_2$ statistics in this $f_3$ equation, let's say by
assuming that A = p4, B = p1, C = p2. When you add up and subtract the paths
from each other, do you arrive at the interpretation of the "outgroup" $f_3$ as
a measure of shared branch between B and C and the "outgroup" A?**

**Then, use the function `ts_f2()` and this equation to compute a "homemade"
$f_3(A = p4; B = p1, C = p2)$ statistic and compare it to the result produced by
`ts_f3()` provided by _slendr_. Do you get the same result?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

First let's get our groups of individuals from all lineages:

```{r}
s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

Now let's compute $f_3$ using the _slendr_ function:

```{r}
ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"])
```

And now let's compose a "homemade" $f_3$ statistic as a linear combination of
$f_2$ statistics as given by the equation:

```{r}
homemade_f3 <- (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"])$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"])$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"])$f2
) / 2

homemade_f3
```

You can see that the `ts_f3()` implementation gives basically the same value as
our "homemade" implementation based on a linear combination of $f_2$ statistics,
just as predicted by the underlying math!

:::



## Exercise: $f_4$ as a measure of overlap of tree paths

The usual application of $f_4$ in practical research usually boils down to some
variant of ABBA/BABA $D$ statistics for testing admixture hypotheses. We will
look at this later, but lets first look at $f_4$ statistics in a more general
case, as a measure of overlapping paths in population trees.

Consider the model from our script `f_statistics.R`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule)
```

```{r}
df <- ts_replicate(n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(model, split = TRUE, schedule = schedule)

  s1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p4"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p1"])
  s2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p4"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p1"])
  s3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p4"], X = s["p1"], Y = s["p4"], Z = s["p2"])

  bind_rows(s1, s2, s3)
})
```

```{r}
p_model1 <- plot_grid(

plot_model(model, schedule = schedule, proportions = TRUE),

ggplot(df, aes(paste(W, X, Y, Z), f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red"),

nrow = 2

)

p_model1
```





```{r}
s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

s1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p4"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p1"])
s2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p4"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p1"])
s3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p4"], X = s["p1"], Y = s["p4"], Z = s["p2"])

bind_rows(s1, s2, s3)
```





## Exercise: $f_4$ as an admixture test

### Branch length overlap as a measure of directionality

#### Base model

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

outgroup <- population("outgroup", time = 7000000, N = 10000)

altai    <- population("Altai",    time = 6000000, N =  1000, parent = outgroup)
vindija  <- population("Vindija",  time =  200000, N =  1000, parent = altai)

san      <- population("San",      time =  600000, N = 10000, parent = altai)
mbuti    <- population("Mbuti",    time =  350000, N = 10000, parent = san)
yoruba   <- population("Yoruba",   time =  220000, N = 10000, parent = mbuti)
dinka    <- population("Dinka",    time =  150000, N = 15000, parent = yoruba)

nonafr   <- population("nonafr",   time =   70000, N = 3000,  parent = dinka)
```

#### Neanderthal -> MH and MH -> Neanderthal gene-flow models

```{r}
model1 <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, altai, vindija, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  gene_flow = gene_flow(from = vindija, to = nonafr, proportion = 0.03, start = 55000, end = 50000),
  generation_time = 30
)
schedule1 <- schedule_recording(model1, times = 0, list("each", 5))

model2 <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, altai, vindija, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  gene_flow = gene_flow(from = nonafr, to = vindija, proportion = 0.03, start = 55000, end = 50000),
  generation_time = 30
)
schedule2 <- schedule_recording(model2, times = 0, list("each", 5))
```

```{r}
plot_grid(
  plot_model(model1, proportions = TRUE, log = TRUE),
  plot_model(model2, proportions = TRUE, log = TRUE)
)
```

```{r}
result1 <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10,
  {
    ts1 <- msprime(model1, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule1) %>% ts_mutate(1e-8)
    
    samples <- ts_names(ts1, split = TRUE)
    
    bind_rows(
      ts_f4(ts1, W = samples["San"],    X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts1, W = samples["Mbuti"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts1, W = samples["Yoruba"], X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts1, W = samples["Dinka"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"])
    )
  }
) %>% mutate(direction = "Nea -> MH")
```

```{r}
result2 <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10,
  {
    ts2 <- msprime(model2, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule1) %>% ts_mutate(1e-8)
    
    samples <- ts_names(ts2, split = TRUE)
    
    bind_rows(
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["San"],    X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Mbuti"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Yoruba"], X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"]),
      ts_f4(ts2, W = samples["Dinka"],  X = samples["nonafr"], Y = samples["Vindija"], Z = samples["outgroup"])
    )
  }
) %>% mutate(direction = "MH -> Nea")
```

```{r}
result <- rbind(result1, result2)
```

```{r}
ggplot(result, aes(W, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ direction)
```




## Exercise: How many unique f4 quartets are there?

If you've learned about $f$-statistics before, you've probably seen various
symmetries in $f_4$ (but also other $f$-statistics) depending on the
arrangement of the "quartet". As a trivial example, an $f_3(A; B, C)$ and
$f_3(A; C, B)$ will give you exactly the same value, and the same thing applies
even to more complex $f$-statistics like $f_4$.

**Use simulations to compute how many unique $f_4$ values involving a single
quartet are there.**

**Hint:** Draw some trees to figure out why could that be true. Also, when
computing `ts_f4()`, set `mode = "branch"` to avoid the effect of statistical
noise due to mutations.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| eval: false
# # install a combinatorics R package
# install.packages("combinat")

library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 4000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

library(combinat)

# These are the four samples we can create quartet combinations from:
quartet <- c("p1_1", "p2_1", "p3_1", "p4_1")

# This is how we can generate all permutations:
quartets <- permn(quartet)
quartets

# How many permutations there are in total?
#   4! = 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 24
factorial(4)

# We should therefore have 24 different quartet combinations of samples
length(quartets)

# Loop across all quartets, computing the corresponding f4 statistic (we want
# to do this using branch lengths, not mutations, as the mutation-based computation
# would involve statistical noise)
all_f4s <- lapply(quartets, function(q) ts_f4(ts, q[1], q[2], q[3], q[4], mode = "branch"))

# Bind the list of f4 results into a single data frame and inspect the results
all_f4s <- bind_rows(all_f4s) %>% arrange(abs(f4))
print(all_f4s, n = Inf)

# Narrow down the results to only unique f4 values
distinct(all_f4s, f4, .keep_all = TRUE)
distinct(all_f4s, abs(f4), .keep_all = TRUE)
```

:::
